title: Regulatory Capture
hook: Who protects a city's drinking water when the industry that put it at risk is also the one the regulator was built to serve? That's the problem political scientists call regulatory capture.
key_points: Regulatory capture is when an agency meant to police an industry starts serving that industry's interests instead.
It often happens gradually: regulators depend on the industry for expertise, jobs, and political support.
Agencies that both promote an industry and police its pollution face a built-in conflict of interest.
A 2026 ProPublica investigation examined an Oklahoma city forced to appeal to oil-and-gas regulators over pollution those regulators had allowed.
The usual remedy reformers push: separate the promoting and policing functions, or add independent outside oversight.
content_html: Regulation only works if the regulator is actually willing to say no to the industry it oversees. Political scientists have a name for what happens when that stops being true: regulatory capture — an agency created to police an industry gradually comes to serve that industry's interests instead, often because it depends on the industry for technical expertise, career pipelines, and political cover.
extra_html: ProPublica's Nick Bowlin and Al Shaw report on a case study of the problem: an Oklahoma city that had to appeal to the same oil-and-gas regulators who had allowed the pollution risk to its drinking water in the first place, in hopes of getting protection from it. Capture is rarely a single corrupt act; it's usually structural, built into agencies whose job combines promoting an industry's growth with policing its harms — a dual mandate that quietly tilts toward the industry over time. The standard reform response is to separate those roles, or to add independent oversight — inspectors general, outside audits, courts — that doesn't share the regulator's day-to-day relationship with the industry it's meant to check.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: Political Corruption
related.hook: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain — and it quietly drains a society, eroding trust, fairness, and the resources meant for everyone.

related.title: Markets, Regulation & the Mixed Economy
related.hook: Pure free market or full state control? Almost every country picks neither — they run a mixed economy, and where they draw the line is one of politics' great arguments.

flashcards.back_html: When an agency created to police an industry comes instead to serve that industry's interests — often because it depends on the industry for expertise and political support.

flashcards.prompt: Why are agencies with a dual mandate (promoting an industry AND policing its harms) especially prone to capture?

choices.text: The dual role creates a built-in conflict of interest that can tilt the agency toward the industry
Dual-mandate agencies are required by law to favor industry
Having two jobs makes an agency more independent

flashcards.explanation_html: Promoting growth and policing harm pull in different directions, and over time the promotion side can quietly win out.

flashcards.prompt: What reform do observers typically propose to counter regulatory capture?

choices.text: Separate the promoting and policing functions, or add independent outside oversight
Eliminate the regulator and let the industry self-report
Merge the regulator fully into the industry it oversees

flashcards.explanation_html: Splitting roles or adding oversight that doesn't share the regulator's close relationship with industry helps counteract the drift toward capture.
